<reflection>
- The first experiment (S=2.0, cat=0.05, P=0.0) resulted in nearly identical negative log-likelihood (NLL) values for almost all 20 models (around -24.1 to -24.5). 
- This indicates that the baseline condition did not sufficiently challenge the models; the more complex models likely reduced to the standard Michaelis-Menten mechanism (M1) by fitting their additional rate constants to near-zero values.
- My aim to establish a baseline was achieved, but it confirms that we must now actively perturb the system to force the models' unique features to manifest.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To differentiate the models, we need an experiment that simultaneously probes multiple distinct mechanistic features (product effects, substrate effects, and catalyst deactivation). 
1. By introducing a high initial product concentration (P=0.5), we will directly test models involving product inhibition or product-induced deactivation (M12, M17, M5). In a standard model, this only slightly shifts the equilibrium, but in M12/M17, it will cause immediate and significant catalyst deactivation.
2. By using the maximum allowable substrate concentration (S=5.0), we will maximize the formation of the `catS` complex and probe substrate inhibition/deactivation pathways (M7, M11, M16).
3. By using a very low catalyst concentration (cat=0.005), the catalyst must undergo 1000 turnovers to consume the substrate. This high turnover requirement acts as an amplifier for any catalyst deactivation mechanisms (M9, M13, M14, M18, M19, M20). Even a very slow deactivation rate will cause the reaction to stall prematurely under these conditions. Additionally, the low catalyst concentration will shift any monomer-dimer equilibria (M2, M3, M13), distinguishing them from higher catalyst concentration regimes.
</hypothesis>
